## **Load Libraries**

```{r}
library("tidyverse")
```

## **Load Data**

```{r}
#| eval: false

dir.create("../data/_raw", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

download.file(
  url      = "https://zenodo.org/records/259661/files/RNA_cqn_matrix.txt.gz?download=1",
  destfile = "../data/_raw/RNA_cqn_matrix.txt.gz",
  mode     = "wb"
)

download.file(
  url      = "https://zenodo.org/records/259661/files/RNA_sample_metadata.txt.gz?download=1",
  destfile = "../data/_raw/RNA_sample_metadata.txt.gz",
  mode     = "wb"
)

download.file(
  url      = "https://zenodo.org/records/259661/files/RNA_count_matrix.txt.gz?download=1",
  destfile = "../data/_raw/RNA_count_matrix.txt.gz",
  mode     = "wb"
)
```

```{r}
# sample meta data
sample_meta <- read_tsv("../data/_raw/RNA_sample_metadata.txt.gz", show_col_types = FALSE)
write_tsv(x = sample_meta, file = "../data/01_sample_meta_load.tsv")

# counts raw data
counts_raw_df <- read.delim("../data/_raw/RNA_count_matrix.txt.gz", check.names = FALSE) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "gene_id")
write_tsv(x = counts_raw_df, file = "../data/01_counts_raw_df_load.tsv")

# counts data normalized
counts_norm_df <- read.delim("../data/_raw/RNA_cqn_matrix.txt.gz", check.names = FALSE) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "gene_id")
write_tsv(x = counts_norm_df, file = "../data/01_counts_norm_df_load.tsv")
```

## Clean Data

### Sample metadata

#### Selection of relevant columns

```{r}
clean_sample_meta <- sample_meta |>
  select(c("sample_id","donor","condition","replicate","condition_name","SL1344","IFNg"                  ,"received_as","mean_purity","max_purity", "sex","rna_concentration"                           ,"purity_bins"
  ))
clean_sample_meta |>
  slice_sample(n = 10)
```

#### Dealing with NAs

Checking which columns contain values at NAs

```{r}
clean_sample_meta |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.))))
```

All missing values were identified in columns related to sample purity. Before deciding how to handle these missing values, we investigated whether their occurrence followed any pattern. For example, if missing values were associated with specific donors, experimental conditions or other sample characteristics.

```{r}
clean_sample_meta |> 
  filter(if_any(contains("purity"), is.na))
```

The NAs are grouped by donor, so the decision was taken to only delete the rows related to the donors that have no data in all columns of purity (filtering with the function `if_all()`) in their samples. This way, we make sure that further analysis is made on reliable data.

```{r}
clean_sample_meta <- clean_sample_meta|>
  filter(!if_all(contains("purity"), is.na))

clean_sample_meta|>
  slice_sample(n=10)
```

#### Fixing columns naming

Two columns had names that were not intuitive or consistent: "SL1344", which indicates whether a sample is a control or was infected with *Salmonella*, and "IFNg", which indicates whether a sample was exposed to IFNγ (primed) or not (naive). To make the dataset easier to understand and keep the naming consistent, these columns were renamed.

```{r}
clean_sample_meta <- clean_sample_meta |>
  rename( 
    SL1344_infection = SL1344,
    IFNg_status = IFNg)

clean_sample_meta|>
  slice_sample(n=10)
```

#### Filter odd data

One more inconsistency was observed. In the column "received_as" we have samples that have the value of "alive/frozen".

First, we investigate how many do we have with this characteristic

```{r}
clean_sample_meta |>
  filter(received_as == "alive/frozen")
```

As we can see from the output, the samples that was received as alive/frozen are from only one donor. For consistency purposes, we decide to also remove the data from this donor.

```{r}
clean_sample_meta <- clean_sample_meta |>
 filter(!received_as == "alive/frozen")
```

### Normalised Counts data

#### Filter low count genes

The authors of the original paper did not filter low-count genes before normalisation (nor do they mention such action), so we used the raw counts to identify them. Genes with consistently low read counts were removed to reduce their influence on the analysis: only genes with at least 10 counts in a minimum of 80 samples were retained

```{r}
clean_counts_raw_df <- counts_raw_df |>
  filter(rowSums(across(-1) >= 10) >= 80)
```

We use `semi_join()` to remove the same genes from the normalised data. This function keeps only the rows of counts_norm whose gene_id also appears in the filtered raw data, without adding any columns from it.

```{r}
clean_counts_norm_df <- counts_norm_df |>
  semi_join(clean_counts_raw_df, by = "gene_id")
```

### Export data

```{r}
write_tsv(x = clean_sample_meta, file = "../data/02_sample_meta_clean.tsv")
write_tsv(x = clean_counts_norm_df, file = "../data/02_counts_norm_clean.tsv")
```

## Augment Data

### Normalised Counts data

The dataset was transformed from wide to long format using `pivot_longer()`. This structure facilitates the integration of the count data with the sample metadata and supports subsequent exploratory analysis and visualization.

```{r}
counts_norm_long <- clean_counts_norm_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = -gene_id,
    names_to  = "sample_id",
    values_to = "log2_counts")

counts_norm_long |>
  slice_sample(n=10)
```

### Creating one data set from two data sets

The two datasets were merged using the sample_id column as a common identifier. The `inner_join()` was used to retain only the samples present in both datasets, ensuring that each gene count was associated with its corresponding sample information.

```{r}
merged_data <- counts_norm_long|>
  inner_join(clean_sample_meta, by = "sample_id")

merged_data |>
  slice_sample(n = 10)
```

#### Consistency in sample_ids

Some sample IDs carried a " \_2 " at the end of the sample id , which marked a replicate and made their format inconsistent with the rest. Now that the datasets are merged, we removed the suffix so all sample IDs follow the same format.

```{r}
merged_data <- merged_data |>
  mutate(sample_id = str_remove(sample_id, "_2"))
```

Checked that each sample appears only once per gene

```{r}
merged_data |>
  count(gene_id, sample_id) |>
  filter(n > 1)
```

### Export Data

```{r}
write_tsv(x = merged_data, file = "../data/02_aug_data.tsv")
```

### Gene summary

```{r}
gene_summary <- merged_data |>
  group_by(gene_id, condition_name) |>
  summarise(
    mean_counts = mean(log2_counts),
    sd_log2_counts   = sd(log2_counts),
    .groups     = "drop"
  ) |>
  drop_na()

gene_summary|>
  slice_sample(n= 10)
```

# Descriptive Analysis of Gene Expression

We wanted to see how gene expression differed across the three experimental conditions. We used the naïve condition as our reference because those cells were neither exposed to IFNγ nor infected with Salmonella. By comparing each condition with the same reference, we could see how large the differences were and how much they varied from gene to gene.

### 1. Mean Expression Differences Relative to Naïve

We used the mean normalized log2 expression values already calculated in gene_summary. To see how each gene’s expression differed from the untreated condition, we matched its mean in each experimental condition with its mean in the naïve condition and subtracted the naïve mean. This gave every gene its own baseline and let us compare how much expression differed across the three conditions. Positive values mean higher expression than in naïve, negative values mean lower expression, and zero means the two means were equal.

```{r}
expression_changes <- gene_summary |>
  select(gene_id, condition_name, mean_counts) |>
  # Put the four condition means side by side for each gene
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = condition_name,
    values_from = mean_counts
  ) |>
  # Create one row per gene and experimental condition
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(IFNg, SL1344, IFNg_SL1344),
    names_to = "condition",
    values_to = "condition_mean"
  ) |>
  mutate(expression_change = condition_mean - naive)

```

### 2. Distribution of Gene Expression Differences

We drew one histogram for each experimental condition. The horizontal axis shows the difference in mean expression from naïve. Each bar counts how many genes had a difference within that range. Taller bars show where more genes are grouped, and a wider histogram shows that the differences are more spread out across genes.

```{r}
# Visualisation with histograms
plot_expression <- expression_changes |>
  ggplot(aes(x = expression_change,
             fill = condition)) +

  geom_histogram(bins = 50,
                 alpha = 0.7) +

  facet_wrap(~ condition,
             nrow = 1) +

  labs(title = "Gene Expression Changes Compared with Naïve",
       x = "Difference in mean normalized log2 expression from naïve",
       y = "Number of genes",
       caption = paste0(
         "Data: Alasoo et al. (2018) | Naïve reference: authors' analysis code\n",
         "Data reshaping: tidyr | Histograms and panels: ggplot2"
       )) +

  theme_minimal() +

  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )

plot_expression
```

### Results

In all three histograms, the tallest bars were close to zero. The IFNγ condition had the narrowest peak, with differences clustered close to zero. The differences were more spread out in the SL1344 condition. The combined IFNγ and SL1344 condition had the widest spread around its peak.

**Exporting the results**

```{r}
# Export the plot
ggsave(
  filename = "../results/04_key_plot_1.png",
  plot     = plot_expression,
  width    = 10,
  height   = 5,
  dpi      = 300
)
```
